samples.text:
The line graph shows the number of cars for each 1,000 people in Germany, South Korea, Turkey and Netherlands between 1970 and 2020.

In 1970 Germany and the Netherlands had much more cars than the other two countries. Germany had 195 cars per 1,000 people and the Netherlands had 180. Both countries increased a lot until 1980, and Germany reached 390 in 1990 and 515 in 2000. The Netherlands was 370 in 1990 and 390 in 2000. In 2020, Germany had 580 cars and the Netherlands had 490.

South Korea and Turkey had almost no cars in 1970, only 2 and 3. South Korea stayed very low until 1980 but then it rised quickly. It was 170 in 2000 and 375 in 2020. Turkey increase more slowly, it had 65 cars in 2000 and 165 in 2020, which was the lowest of all countries.

Overall, car ownership was going up in all countries. Germany had the most cars in all the period and South Korea have the fastest growth.
samples.why: Basic overview at the end · key features covered with list-like figures · adequate vocabulary · errors in comparatives, past tense forms and agreement that do not obscure meaning.

samples.text:
The graph illustrates the number of cars owned per 1,000 people in four countries, Germany, South Korea, Turkey and the Netherlands, over a fifty-year period from 1970.

Overall, car ownership increased considerably in all four countries. Germany and the Netherlands had far higher rates than the other two for the whole period, although South Korea narrowed the gap significantly after 1990, while Turkey remained well behind.

In 1970, there were 195 cars per 1,000 people in Germany and 180 in the Netherlands. Both countries saw rapid growth during the 1970s, reaching 330 and 320 respectively in 1980. From then on, Germany generally pulled ahead, climbing to 515 in 2000 and 580 in 2020, whereas the Dutch figure rose more gradually to 490.

In contrast, cars were very rare in South Korea and Turkey in 1970, with only 2 and 3 cars per 1,000 people. Turkey was slightly ahead in 1980, but South Korea overtook it by 1990 and then grew remarkably fast, reaching 375 by 2020. Turkey's increase was steadier and more modest, and at 165 it still had the lowest level of car ownership at the end of the period.
samples.why: Clear overview with main groupings · key features and the crossover highlighted · logical progression · good range of cohesive devices · mostly error-free, with an occasional imprecise word choice.

samples.text:
The graph charts levels of car ownership, expressed as cars per 1,000 people, in Germany, South Korea, Turkey and the Netherlands between 1970 and 2020.

Overall, car ownership rose substantially in every country. Germany and the Netherlands started from a much higher base and remained ahead throughout, but South Korea closed much of the gap in the later decades, while Turkey's growth, though steady, left it with the lowest rate by some distance.

The two European countries initially had similar levels, with 195 and 180 cars per 1,000 people respectively in 1970, and both rose sharply over the following decade. Thereafter their paths diverged somewhat: ownership in Germany jumped to 515 by 2000 and, after a slight dip in 2010, reached 580 in 2020, whereas the Netherlands experienced slower growth, finishing on 490.

In 1970, by contrast, cars were a rarity in South Korea and Turkey, with just 2 and 3 per 1,000 people. Turkey held a slight lead until 1980, but South Korea subsequently surged ahead, with ownership rising more than sevenfold between 1990 and 2020 to 375. Turkey's figure climbed far more gradually, reaching 165 by the end of the period.
samples.why: Key features skilfully selected, including divergence and South Korea's catch-up · clear overview · accurate figures with valid derived comparison · wide, precise vocabulary · wide range of accurate structures.
